Pull Requests that add support for new targets to `getrandom` are always welcome.

[§](https://docs.rs#opt-in-backends)Opt-in backends

`getrandom` also provides optional (opt-in) backends, which allow users to customize the source
of randomness based on their specific needs:

| Backend name | Target | Target Triple | Implementation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `linux_getrandom` | Linux, Android | `*‑linux‑*` | system call (without`getrandom``/dev/urandom`fallback). Bumps minimum supported Linux kernel version to 3.17 and Android API level to 23 (Marshmallow). |
| `linux_raw` | Linux, Android | `*‑linux‑*` | Same as `linux_getrandom`, but uses raw`asm!`-based syscalls instead of`libc`. |
| `rdrand` | x86, x86-64 | `x86_64-*`,`i686-*` | instruction`RDRAND` |
| `rndr` | AArch64 | `aarch64-*` | register`RNDR` |
| `wasm_js` | Web Browser, Node.js | `wasm32‑unknown‑unknown`,`wasm32v1-none` | . Enabled by the`Crypto.getRandomValues``wasm_js`feature ([see below](https://docs.rs#webassembly-support)). |
| `efi_rng` | UEFI | `*-unknown‑uefi` | with`EFI_RNG_PROTOCOL``EFI_RNG_ALGORITHM_RAW`(requires`std`and Nightly compiler) |
| `windows_legacy` | Windows | `*-windows-*` | `RtlGenRandom` |
| `custom` | All targets | `*` | User-provided custom implementation (see [custom backend](https://docs.rs#custom-backend)) |
| `unsupported` | All targets | `*` | Always returns `Err(Error::UNSUPPORTED)`(see[unsupported backend](https://docs.rs#unsupported-backend)) |

Opt-in backends can be enabled using the `getrandom_backend` configuration flag.
The flag can be set either by specifying the `rustflags` field in [ .cargo/config.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html):

```
# It's recommended to set the flag on a per-target basis:
[target.wasm32-unknown-unknown]
rustflags = ['--cfg', 'getrandom_backend="wasm_js"']
```
Or by using the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable:

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg getrandom_backend="linux_getrandom"' cargo build`Enabling an opt-in backend will replace the backend used by default. Doing this for
an incorrect target (e.g. using `linux_getrandom` while compiling for a Windows target)
will result in a compilation error. Be extremely careful while using opt-in backends,
as incorrect configuration may result in vulnerable applications or applications
that always panic.

Note that using an opt-in backend in a library (e.g. for tests or benchmarks) WILL NOT have any effect on its downstream users.

[§](https://docs.rs#raw-linux-syscall-support)Raw Linux syscall support

Currently the `linux_raw` backend supports only targets with stabilized `asm!` macro,
i.e. `arm`, `aarch64`, `loongarch64`, `riscv32`, `riscv64`, `s390x`, `x86`, and `x86_64`.

Note that the raw syscall backend may be slower than backends based on `libc::getrandom`,
e.g. it does not implement vDSO optimizations and on `x86` it uses the infamously slow
`int 0x80` instruction to perform syscall.

[§](https://docs.rs#webassembly-support)WebAssembly support

This crate fully supports the [WASI](https://github.com/WebAssembly/WASI) and [Emscripten](https://emscripten.org) targets. However,
the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target (i.e. the target used by `wasm-pack`)
is not automatically supported since, from the target name alone, we cannot deduce
which JavaScript interface should be used (or if JavaScript is available at all).

We do not include support for this target in the default configuration because
our JS backend (supporting web browsers, web workers and Node.js v19 or later)
requires [ wasm-bindgen](https://github.com/rustwasm/wasm-bindgen),

**bloating**and

`Cargo.lock`**potentially breaking builds**on non-web WASM platforms.

To enable `getrandom`’s functionality on `wasm32-unknown-unknown` using the Web
Crypto methods [described above](https://docs.rs#opt-in-backends) via [ wasm-bindgen](https://github.com/rustwasm/wasm-bindgen), enable the

`wasm_js` feature flag. Setting `RUSTFLAGS='--cfg getrandom_backend="wasm_js"'`
is allowed but is no longer required and does nothing (it was required in a
prior version of this crate).WARNING: enabling the `wasm_js` feature will bloat `Cargo.lock` on all platforms
(where [ wasm-bindgen](https://github.com/rustwasm/wasm-bindgen) is not an existing dependency) and is known to cause
build issues on some non-web WASM platforms, even when a different backend is
selected via

`getrandom_backend`.[§](https://docs.rs#custom-backend)Custom backend

If this crate does not support your target out of the box or you have to use
a non-default entropy source, then you can provide a custom implementation.
You need to enable the custom backend as described in the
[opt-in backends](https://docs.rs#opt-in-backends) section.

Next, you need to define an `extern` function with the following signature:

```
use getrandom::Error;
#[no_mangle]
unsafe extern "Rust" fn __getrandom_v03_custom(
    dest: *mut u8,
    len: usize,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    todo!()
}
```
This function should, ideally, be defined in the root crate of your project,
e.g. in your `main.rs`. This function MUST be defined only once for your
project, i.e. upstream library crates SHOULD NOT define it outside of
tests and benchmarks. Improper configuration of this backend may result
in linking errors.

The function accepts a pointer to a buffer that should be filled with random
data and its length in bytes. Note that the buffer MAY be uninitialized.
On success, the function should return `Ok(())` and fully fill the input buffer;
otherwise, it should return an error value.

While wrapping functions which work with byte slices you should fully initialize the buffer before passing it to the function:

```
use getrandom::Error;
fn my_entropy_source(buf: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), getrandom::Error> {
    // ...
    Ok(())
}
#[no_mangle]
unsafe extern "Rust" fn __getrandom_v03_custom(
    dest: *mut u8,
    len: usize,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let buf = unsafe {
        // fill the buffer with zeros
        core::ptr::write_bytes(dest, 0, len);
        // create mutable byte slice
        core::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(dest, len)
    };
    my_entropy_source(buf)
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#unsupported-backend)Unsupported backend

In some rare scenarios, you might be compiling this crate for an unsupported
target (e.g. `wasm32-unknown-unknown`), but this crate’s functionality
is not actually used by your code. If you are confident that `getrandom` is
not used in your project, but it gets pulled nevertheless by one of your
dependencies, then you can enable the `unsupported` backend, which always
returns `Err(Error::UNSUPPORTED)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-support)Platform Support

This crate generally supports the same operating system and platform versions that the Rust standard library does. Additional targets may be supported using the opt-in custom backend.

This means that as Rust drops support for old versions of operating systems
(such as old Linux kernel versions, Android API levels, etc.) in stable releases,
`getrandom` may create new patch releases that remove support for
outdated platform versions.

[§](https://docs.rs#devurandom-fallback-on-linux-and-android)`/dev/urandom` fallback on Linux and Android

On Linux targets, the `/dev/urandom` fallback is present only if either `target_env`
is `musl`, or `target_arch` is one of the following: `aarch64`, `arm`, `powerpc`,
`powerpc64`, `s390x`, `x86`, `x86_64`. Other supported targets [require](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/rustc/platform-support.html)
kernel versions that support the `getrandom` system call, so the fallback is not needed.

On Android targets the fallback is present only for the following `target_arch`es:
`aarch64`, `arm`, `x86`, `x86_64`. Other `target_arch`es (e.g. RISC-V) require
sufficiently high API levels.

The fallback can be disabled by enabling the `linux_getrandom` opt-in backend.
Note that doing so will bump minimum supported Linux kernel version to 3.17
and Android API level to 23 (Marshmallow).

[§](https://docs.rs#early-boot)Early boot

Sometimes, early in the boot process, the OS has not collected enough entropy to securely seed its RNG. This is especially common on virtual machines, where standard “random” events are hard to come by.

Some operating system interfaces always block until the RNG is securely seeded. This can take anywhere from a few seconds to more than a minute. A few (Linux, NetBSD and Solaris) offer a choice between blocking and getting an error; in these cases, we always choose to block.

On Linux (when the `getrandom` system call is not available), reading from
`/dev/urandom` never blocks, even when the OS hasn’t collected enough
entropy yet. To avoid returning low-entropy bytes, we first poll
`/dev/random` and only switch to `/dev/urandom` once this has succeeded.

On OpenBSD, this kind of entropy accounting isn’t available, and on NetBSD, blocking on it is discouraged. On these platforms, nonblocking interfaces are used, even when reliable entropy may not be available. On the platforms where it is used, the reliability of entropy accounting itself isn’t free from controversy. This library provides randomness sourced according to the platform’s best practices, but each platform has its own limits on the grade of randomness it can promise in environments with few sources of entropy.

On ESP-IDF, if `esp_fill_random` is used before enabling WiFi, BT, or the
voltage noise entropy source (SAR ADC), the Hardware RNG will only be seeded
via RC_FAST_CLK. This can occur during early boot unless
`bootloader_random_enable()` is called. For more information see the
[ESP-IDF RNG Docs](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/api-reference/system/random.html) or the
[RNG section of the ESP32 Technical Reference Manual](https://www.espressif.com/sites/default/files/documentation/esp32_technical_reference_manual_en.pdf#rng).

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling)Error handling

We always prioritize failure over returning known insecure “random” bytes.
Generally, on supported platforms, failure is highly unlikely, though not
impossible. If an error does occur, it is likely that it will occur
on every call to `getrandom`. Therefore, after the first successful call,
one can be reasonably confident that no errors will occur.

[§](https://docs.rs#panic-handling)Panic handling

We strive to eliminate all potential panics from our backend implementations.
In other words, when compiled with optimizations enabled, the generated
binary code for `getrandom` functions should not contain any panic branches.
Even if the platform misbehaves and returns an unexpected result,
our code should correctly handle it and return an error, e.g.
[ Error::UNEXPECTED](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html#associatedconstant.UNEXPECTED).

[§](https://docs.rs#sanitizer-support)Sanitizer support

If your code uses [ fill_uninit](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_uninit.html) and you enable

[MemorySanitizer](https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/unstable-book/compiler-flags/sanitizer.html#memorysanitizer)(i.e.

`-Zsanitizer=memory`), we will automatically handle unpoisoning
of the destination buffer filled by `fill_uninit`.You can run sanitizer tests for your crate dependent on `getrandom` like this:

`RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=memory" cargo test -Zbuild-std --target=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

This crate requires Rust 1.63 or later.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

The `getrandom` library is distributed under either of

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribution)Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.9/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// The prelude import enables methods we use below, specifically
// Rng::random, Rng::sample, SliceRandom::shuffle and IndexedRandom::choose.
use rand::prelude::*;
// Get an RNG:
let mut rng = rand::rng();
// Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
println!("char: '{}'", rng.random::<char>());
// Try printing a random alphanumeric value instead!
println!("alpha: '{}'", rng.sample(rand::distr::Alphanumeric) as char);
// Generate and shuffle a sequence:
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
// And take a random pick (yes, we didn't need to shuffle first!):
let _ = nums.choose(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

# wyhash - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wyhash/^0.6/

## Expand description

Rust implementation of the [wyhash algorithm by Wang Yi](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash).

The hashing algorithm passes SMHasher and the random number generator
passes BigCrush and practrand.
As of now it is the fastest algorithm in the SMHasher benchmark
(faster than t1ha and XXH3).
See [here](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash).

Furthermore, this algorithm is solid, simple, portable (does not need
hardware support, can be used in `no_std` environments) and has
no dependencies.

The generated hashes are equal (see tests) as of the version stated
[here](https://github.com/eldruin/wyhash-rs/blob/master/comparison/original/CMakeLists.txt) although the speed varies
([PRs are welcome](https://github.com/eldruin/wyhash-rs/issues)).

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

By default this crate uses 128-bit integer multiplications.
To restrict that to 64 bits you can enable the feature `mum32bit`. This offers better
performance on 32-bit architectures.
Beware that this feature produces different the results.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage-see-also-examples-folder)Usage (see also examples folder)

For the hashing function you can use either the free function or the
`Hasher` trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#wyhash-function-usage)`wyhash` function usage

```
use wyhash::wyhash;
let data = [0, 1, 2];
let seed = 3;
let hash = wyhash(&data, seed);
println!("{:x}", hash); // prints b0f941520b1ad95d
```
[§](https://docs.rs#hasher-trait-usage)`Hasher` trait usage

You can also use `std::hash::Hasher`, it is the same.

```
use core::hash::Hasher;
use wyhash::WyHash;
let mut hasher = WyHash::with_seed(3);
hasher.write(&[0, 1, 2]);
println!("{:x}", hasher.finish()); // prints b0f941520b1ad95d
```
[§](https://docs.rs#wyrng-function-usage)`wyrng` function usage

Note that the seed parameter is updated so that it is possible to generate a sequence of random numbers.

```
use wyhash::wyrng;
let mut seed = 3;
let random_number = wyrng(&mut seed);
println!("{:x}", random_number); // prints 3e99a772750dcbe
println!("{:x}", seed); //prints a0761d6478bd6432
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rngcore-trait-usage)`RngCore` trait usage

You can also use `rand::Rng`, it is the same.

```
use rand_core::RngCore;
use wyhash::WyRng;
let mut rng = WyRng::default();
println!("{:x}", rng.next_u64()); // prints 111cb3a78f59a58e
```
[§](https://docs.rs#seedablerng-trait-usage)`SeedableRng` trait usage

You can also use `rand::SeedableRng`, it is the same.

```
use rand_core::{RngCore, SeedableRng};
use wyhash::WyRng;
// Seeds are 8-byte long.
let seed = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7];
let mut rng1 = WyRng::from_seed(seed);
println!("{:x}", rng1.next_u64()); // prints d730135774c6ae31
// Alternatively you can also use this convenience method:
let mut rng2 = WyRng::seed_from_u64(3);
println!("{:x}", rng2.next_u64()); // prints 3e99a772750dcbe
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::v1::`- [wyhash](https://docs.rs/v1/fn.wyhash.html);
- `pub use crate::v1::`- [wyrng](https://docs.rs/v1/fn.wyrng.html);
- `pub use crate::v1::`- [WyHash](https://docs.rs/v1/struct.WyHash.html);
- `pub use crate::v1::`- [WyHasherBuilder](https://docs.rs/v1/struct.WyHasherBuilder.html);
- `pub use crate::v1::`- [WyRng](https://docs.rs/v1/struct.WyRng.html);

# fastrand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fastrand/2.4.1/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/fastrand/

## Expand description

A simple and fast random number generator.

The implementation uses [Wyrand](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash), a simple and fast
generator but **not** cryptographically secure.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Flip a coin:

```
if fastrand::bool() {
    println!("heads");
} else {
    println!("tails");
}
```
Generate a random `i32`:

`let num = fastrand::i32(..);`Choose a random element in an array:

```
let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let i = fastrand::usize(..v.len());
let elem = v[i];
```
Sample values from an array with `O(n)` complexity (`n` is the length of array):

```
fastrand::choose_multiple([1, 4, 5], 2);
fastrand::choose_multiple(0..20, 12);
```
Shuffle an array:

```
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
fastrand::shuffle(&mut v);
```
Generate a random [ Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html) or

[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String````
use std::iter::repeat_with;
let v: Vec<i32> = repeat_with(|| fastrand::i32(..)).take(10).collect();
let s: String = repeat_with(fastrand::alphanumeric).take(10).collect();
```
To get reproducible results on every run, initialize the generator with a seed:

```
// Pick an arbitrary number as seed.
fastrand::seed(7);
// Now this prints the same number on every run:
println!("{}", fastrand::u32(..));
```
To be more efficient, create a new [ Rng](https://docs.rs/struct.Rng.html) instance instead of using the thread-local
generator:

```
use std::iter::repeat_with;
let mut rng = fastrand::Rng::new();
let mut bytes: Vec<u8> = repeat_with(|| rng.u8(..)).take(10_000).collect();
```
This crate aims to expose a core set of useful randomness primitives. For more niche algorithms,
consider using the [ fastrand-contrib](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand-contrib) crate alongside this one.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `std`(enabled by default): Enables the- `std`library. This is required for the global generator and global entropy. Without this feature,- `Rng`- `with_seed`
- `js`: Assumes that WebAssembly targets are being run in a JavaScript environment. See the- [WebAssembly Notes](https://docs.rs#webassembly-notes)section for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#webassembly-notes)WebAssembly Notes

For non-WASI WASM targets, there is additional subtlety to consider when utilizing the global RNG.
By default, `std` targets will use entropy sources in the standard library to seed the global RNG.
However, these sources are not available by default on WASM targets outside of WASI.

If the `js` feature is enabled, this crate will assume that it is running in a JavaScript
environment. At this point, the [ getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom) crate will be used in order to access the available
entropy sources and seed the global RNG. If the

`js` feature is not enabled, the global RNG will
use a predefined seed.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Rng](https://docs.rs/struct.Rng.html)
- A random number generator.

# fastrand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fastrand/2.4.1/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/fastrand/

## Expand description

A simple and fast random number generator.

The implementation uses [Wyrand](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash), a simple and fast
generator but **not** cryptographically secure.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Flip a coin:

```
if fastrand::bool() {
    println!("heads");
} else {
    println!("tails");
}
```
Generate a random `i32`:

`let num = fastrand::i32(..);`Choose a random element in an array:

```
let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let i = fastrand::usize(..v.len());
let elem = v[i];
```
Sample values from an array with `O(n)` complexity (`n` is the length of array):

```
fastrand::choose_multiple([1, 4, 5], 2);
fastrand::choose_multiple(0..20, 12);
```
Shuffle an array:

```
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
fastrand::shuffle(&mut v);
```
Generate a random [ Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html) or

[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String````
use std::iter::repeat_with;
let v: Vec<i32> = repeat_with(|| fastrand::i32(..)).take(10).collect();
let s: String = repeat_with(fastrand::alphanumeric).take(10).collect();
```
To get reproducible results on every run, initialize the generator with a seed:

```
// Pick an arbitrary number as seed.
fastrand::seed(7);
// Now this prints the same number on every run:
println!("{}", fastrand::u32(..));
```
To be more efficient, create a new [ Rng](https://docs.rs/struct.Rng.html) instance instead of using the thread-local
generator:

```
use std::iter::repeat_with;
let mut rng = fastrand::Rng::new();
let mut bytes: Vec<u8> = repeat_with(|| rng.u8(..)).take(10_000).collect();
```
This crate aims to expose a core set of useful randomness primitives. For more niche algorithms,
consider using the [ fastrand-contrib](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand-contrib) crate alongside this one.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `std`(enabled by default): Enables the- `std`library. This is required for the global generator and global entropy. Without this feature,- `Rng`- `with_seed`
- `js`: Assumes that WebAssembly targets are being run in a JavaScript environment. See the- [WebAssembly Notes](https://docs.rs#webassembly-notes)section for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#webassembly-notes)WebAssembly Notes

For non-WASI WASM targets, there is additional subtlety to consider when utilizing the global RNG.
By default, `std` targets will use entropy sources in the standard library to seed the global RNG.
However, these sources are not available by default on WASM targets outside of WASI.

If the `js` feature is enabled, this crate will assume that it is running in a JavaScript
environment. At this point, the [ getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom) crate will be used in order to access the available
entropy sources and seed the global RNG. If the

`js` feature is not enabled, the global RNG will
use a predefined seed.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# Rng in fastrand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fastrand/^2.0.1/struct.Rng.html

`pub struct Rng(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A random number generator.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new random number generator with the initial seed.

Clones the generator by deterministically deriving a new generator based on the initial seed.

This function can be used to create a new generator that is a “spinoff” of the old generator. The new generator will not produce the same sequence of values as the old generator.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Seed two generators equally, and clone both of them.
let mut base1 = fastrand::Rng::with_seed(0x4d595df4d0f33173);
base1.bool(); // Use the generator once.
let mut base2 = fastrand::Rng::with_seed(0x4d595df4d0f33173);
base2.bool(); // Use the generator once.
let mut rng1 = base1.fork();
let mut rng2 = base2.fork();
println!("rng1 returns {}", rng1.u32(..));
println!("rng2 returns {}", rng2.u32(..));
```
Generates a random digit in the given `base`.

Digits are represented by `char`s in ranges 0-9 and a-z.

Panics if the base is zero or greater than 36.

Generates a random `f32` in range `0..1`.

Function `f32_inclusive()` is a little simpler and faster, so default
to that if inclusive range is acceptable.

Generates a random `f64` in range `0..1`.

Function `f64_inclusive()` is a little simpler and faster, so default
to that if inclusive range is acceptable.

#### pub fn [choose_multiple](https://docs.rs#method.choose_multiple)<I: [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)>(
    &mut self,
    source: I,
    amount: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<I::[Item](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html#associatedtype.Item)>

**crate feature**only.

`alloc`Collects `amount` values at random from the iterable into a vector.

The length of the returned vector equals `amount` unless the iterable
contains insufficient elements, in which case it equals the number of
elements available.

Complexity is `O(n)` where `n` is the length of the iterable.

# camino_tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino-tempfile/latest/target-redirect/camino_tempfile/index.html

## Expand description

Temporary files and directories with UTF-8 paths.

`camino-tempfile` is a wrapper around the [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tempfile/index.html) crate that returns

[rather than](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)

`Path`If your code mostly uses [ camino](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/index.html), it can be annoying to have to convert temporary paths to

`Utf8Path` over and over again. This crate takes care of that for you.This library and its documentation are adapted from the [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/tempfile/3.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tempfile/index.html) crate, and
are used under the MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses.

This crate closely mirrors tempfile’s interface. For extensions that provide
quality-of-life improvements such as the ability to create files easily, see
[ camino-tempfile-ext](https://crates.io/crates/camino-tempfile-ext).

[§](https://docs.rs#synopsis)Synopsis

- Use the `tempfile()`
- Use the `tempdir()`

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html)

`Utf8TempDir`[both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)

`NamedUtf8TempFile`When choosing between the temporary file variants, prefer `tempfile` unless you either need to
know the file’s path or to be able to persist it.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However,

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html)

`Utf8TempDir`[will fail if their destructors don’t run. This is because](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)

`NamedUtf8TempFile`[relies on the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html)

`tempfile()`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html)

`Utf8TempDir`[rely on Rust destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled signal interrupt (like](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)

`NamedUtf8TempFile``SIGINT`), or if the instance is
declared statically, among other possible reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.

[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) doesn’t rely on file paths so this isn’t an issue. However,

[does rely on file paths for](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)

`NamedUtf8TempFile`*some*operations. See the security documentation on the

[type for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)

`NamedUtf8TempFile`[§](https://docs.rs#early-drop-pitfall)Early drop pitfall

Because [ Utf8TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html) and

[rely on their destructors for cleanup, this can lead to an unexpected early removal of the directory/file, usually when working with APIs which are generic over](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)

`NamedUtf8TempFile``AsRef<Utf8Path>` or `AsRef<Path>`. Consider the following example:```
// Create a directory inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`.
let temp_dir = tempdir()?;
// Spawn the `touch` command inside the temporary directory and collect the exit status
// Note that `temp_dir` is **not** moved into `current_dir`, but passed as a reference
let exit_status = Command::new("touch").arg("tmp").current_dir(&temp_dir).status()?;
assert!(exit_status.success());
```
This works because a reference to `temp_dir` is passed to `current_dir`, resulting in the
destructor of `temp_dir` being run after the `Command` has finished execution. Moving the
[ Utf8TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html) into the

`current_dir` call would result in the [being converted into an internal representation, with the original value being dropped and the directory thus being deleted, before the command can be executed.](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html)

`Utf8TempDir`The `touch` command would fail with an `No such file or directory` error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use camino_tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::{self, Write};
// Create a file inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Create a named temporary file and open an independent file handle:

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
use std::io::{self, Write, Read};
let text = "Brian was here. Briefly.";
// Create a file inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file1 = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
// Re-open it.
let mut file2 = file1.reopen()?;
// Write some test data to the first handle.
file1.write_all(text.as_bytes())?;
// Read the test data using the second handle.
let mut buf = String::new();
file2.read_to_string(&mut buf)?;
assert_eq!(buf, text);
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use camino_tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{self, Write};
// Create a directory inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`.
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `Utf8TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

# tempfile in camino_tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino-tempfile/latest/target-redirect/camino_tempfile/fn.tempfile.html

## Expand description

Create a new temporary file.

The file will be created in the location returned by [ std::env::temp_dir()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.temp_dir.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This variant is secure/reliable in the presence of a pathological temporary file cleaner.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

The temporary file will be automatically removed by the OS when the last handle to it is closed. This doesn’t rely on Rust destructors being run, so will (almost) never fail to clean up the temporary file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the file can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::{self, Write};
// Create a file inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```

# tempdir in camino_tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino-tempfile/latest/target-redirect/camino_tempfile/fn.tempdir.html

`pub fn tempdir() -> `[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[Utf8TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html)>## Expand description

Create a new temporary directory.

The `tempdir` function creates a directory in the file system and returns a [ Utf8TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html). The
directory will be automatically deleted when the

[’s destructor is run.](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html)

`Utf8TempDir`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

See [the resource leaking](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html#resource-leaking) docs on `Utf8TempDir`.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the directory can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{self, Write};
// Create a directory inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// `tmp_dir` goes out of scope, the directory as well as
// `tmp_file` will be deleted here.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

# Utf8TempDir in camino_tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino-tempfile/latest/target-redirect/camino_tempfile/struct.Utf8TempDir.html

`pub struct Utf8TempDir { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A directory in the filesystem that is automatically deleted when it goes out of scope.

The [ Utf8TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html) type creates a directory on the file system that is deleted once it goes out
of scope. At construction, the

[creates a new directory with a randomly generated name.](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html)

`Utf8TempDir`The default constructor, [ Utf8TempDir::new()](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html#method.new), creates directories in the location returned by

[, but](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`std::env::temp_dir()``Utf8TempDir` can be configured to manage a temporary directory in
any location by constructing with a [.](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html)

`Builder`After creating a `Utf8TempDir`, work with the file system by doing standard [ std::fs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/index.html) file
system operations on its

[, which can be retrieved with](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)

`Utf8Path`[. Once the](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html#method.path)

`Utf8TempDir::path()``Utf8TempDir` value is dropped, the directory at the path will be deleted, along with any
files and directories it contains. It is your responsibility to ensure that no further file
system operations are attempted inside the temporary directory once it has been deleted.[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

Various platform-specific conditions may cause `Utf8TempDir` to fail to delete the underlying
directory. It’s important to ensure that handles (like [ File](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html) and

[) to files inside the directory are dropped before the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.ReadDir.html)

`ReadDir``TempDir`
goes out of scope. The `Utf8TempDir` destructor will silently ignore any errors in deleting the
directory; to instead handle errors call [.](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html#method.close)

`Utf8TempDir::close()`Note that if the program exits before the `Utf8TempDir` destructor is run, such as via
[ std::process::exit()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/fn.exit.html), by segfaulting, or by receiving a signal like

`SIGINT`, then the
temporary directory will not be deleted.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary directory with a generated name:

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
use camino_tempfile::Utf8TempDir;
// Create a directory inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`
let tmp_dir = Utf8TempDir::new()?;
```
Create a temporary directory with a prefix in its name:

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
use camino_tempfile::Builder;
// Create a directory inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`,
// whose name will begin with 'example'.
let tmp_dir = Builder::new().prefix("example").tempdir()?;
```

Attempts to make a temporary directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.

See [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) for more configuration.

The directory and everything inside it will be automatically deleted once the returned
`Utf8TempDir` is destroyed.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the directory can not be created, or if `env::temp_dir` is a non-UTF-8 path, `Err` is
returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
use camino_tempfile::Utf8TempDir;
// Create a directory inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`
let tmp_dir = Utf8TempDir::new()?;
let file_path = tmp_dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut tmp_file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(tmp_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// `tmp_dir` goes out of scope, the directory as well as
// `tmp_file` will be deleted here.
```

```
use camino_tempfile::Utf8TempDir;
let tmp_path;
{
   let tmp_dir = Utf8TempDir::new()?;
   tmp_path = tmp_dir.path().to_owned();
   // Check that the temp directory actually exists.
   assert!(tmp_path.exists());
   // End of `tmp_dir` scope, directory will be deleted
}
// Temp directory should be deleted by now
assert_eq!(tmp_path.exists(), false);
```

#### pub fn [keep](https://docs.rs#method.keep)(self) -> [Utf8PathBuf](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html)

Persist the temporary directory to disk, returning the [ Utf8PathBuf](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8PathBuf.html) where it is located.

This consumes the [ Utf8TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html) without deleting directory on the filesystem, meaning that
the directory will no longer be automatically deleted.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use std::fs;
use camino_tempfile::Utf8TempDir;
let tmp_dir = Utf8TempDir::new()?;
// Persist the temporary directory to disk,
// getting the path where it is.
let tmp_path = tmp_dir.keep();
// Delete the temporary directory ourselves.
fs::remove_dir_all(tmp_path)?;
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camino_tempfile/dir.rs.html#433-435)#### pub fn [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#method.disable_cleanup)(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camino_tempfile/dir.rs.html#433-435)

#### pub fn [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#method.disable_cleanup)(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Disable cleanup of the temporary directory. If `disable_cleanup` is
`true`, the temporary directory will not be deleted when this
`Utf8TempDir` is dropped. This method is equivalent to calling
[ Builder::disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.disable_cleanup) when creating the

`Utf8TempDir`.**NOTE:** this method is primarily useful for testing/debugging. If you
want to simply turn a temporary directory into a non-temporary
directory, prefer [ Utf8TempDir::keep](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html#method.keep).

Closes and removes the temporary directory, returning a `Result`.

Although `Utf8TempDir` removes the directory on drop, in the destructor any errors are
ignored. To detect errors cleaning up the temporary directory, call `close` instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-6)Errors

This function may return a variety of [ std::io::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)s that result from deleting the
files and directories contained with the temporary directory, as well as from deleting the
temporary directory itself. These errors may be platform specific.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
use camino_tempfile::Utf8TempDir;
// Create a directory inside of `std::env::temp_dir()`.
let tmp_dir = Utf8TempDir::new()?;
let file_path = tmp_dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut tmp_file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(tmp_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `Utf8TempDir` explicitly we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `tmp_dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(tmp_file);
tmp_dir.close()?;
```

# NamedUtf8TempFile in camino_tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino-tempfile/latest/target-redirect/camino_tempfile/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html

`pub struct NamedUtf8TempFile<F = `[File](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

A named temporary file.

The default constructor, [ NamedUtf8TempFile::new()](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html#method.new), creates files in
the location returned by

[, but](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`std::env::temp_dir()``NamedUtf8TempFile`
can be configured to manage a temporary file in any location
by constructing with [.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html#method.new_in)

`NamedUtf8TempFile::new_in()`[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

Most operating systems employ temporary file cleaners to delete old
temporary files. Unfortunately these temporary file cleaners don’t always
reliably *detect* whether the temporary file is still being used.

Specifically, the following sequence of events can happen:

- A user creates a temporary file with `NamedUtf8TempFile::new()`.
- Time passes.
- The temporary file cleaner deletes (unlinks) the temporary file from the filesystem.
- Some other program creates a new file to replace this deleted temporary file.
- The user tries to re-open the temporary file (in the same program or in a different program) by path. Unfortunately, they’ll end up opening the file created by the other program, not the original file.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-system-specific-concerns)Operating System Specific Concerns

The behavior of temporary files and temporary file cleaners differ by operating system.

[§](https://docs.rs#windows)Windows

On Windows, open files *can’t* be deleted. This removes most of the concerns
around temporary file cleaners.

Furthermore, temporary files are, by default, created in per-user temporary
file directories so only an application running as the same user would be
able to interfere (which they could do anyways). However, an application
running as the same user can still *accidentally* re-create deleted
temporary files if the number of random bytes in the temporary file name is
too small.

So, the only real concern on Windows is:

- Opening a named temporary file in a world-writable directory.
- Using the `into_temp_path()`and/or`into_parts()`APIs to close the file handle without deleting the underlying file.
- Continuing to use the file by path.

[§](https://docs.rs#unix)UNIX

Unlike on Windows, UNIX (and UNIX like) systems allow open files to be “unlinked” (deleted).

[§](https://docs.rs#macos)MacOS

Like on Windows, temporary files are created in per-user temporary file
directories by default so calling `NamedUtf8TempFile::new()` should be
relatively safe.

[§](https://docs.rs#linux)Linux

Unfortunately, most *Linux* distributions don’t create per-user temporary
file directories. Worse, systemd’s tmpfiles daemon (a common temporary file
cleaner) will happily remove open temporary files if they haven’t been
modified within the last 10 days.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

If the program exits before the `NamedUtf8TempFile` destructor is
run, the temporary file will not be deleted. This can happen
if the process exits using [ std::process::exit()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/fn.exit.html), a segfault occurs,
receiving an interrupt signal like

`SIGINT` that is not handled, or by using
a statically declared `NamedUtf8TempFile` instance (like with `lazy_static`).Use the [ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) function unless you need a named file path.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camino_tempfile/file.rs.html#590-592)#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)() -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedUtf8TempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camino_tempfile/file.rs.html#590-592)

#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)() -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedUtf8TempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)>

Create a new named temporary file.

See [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) for more configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-1)Security

This will create a temporary file in the default temporary file directory (platform dependent). This has security implications on many platforms so please read the security section of this type’s documentation.

Reasons to use this method:

-
The file has a short lifetime and your temporary file cleaner is sane (doesn’t delete recently accessed files).
-
You trust every user on your system (i.e. you are the only user).
-
You have disabled your system’s temporary file cleaner or verified that your system doesn’t have a temporary file cleaner.

Reasons not to use this method:

-
You’ll fix it later. No you won’t.
-
You don’t care about the security of the temporary file. If none of the “reasons to use this method” apply, referring to a temporary file by name may allow an attacker to create/overwrite your non-temporary files. There are exceptions but if you don’t already know them, don’t use this method.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the file can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a named temporary file and write some data to it:

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
let mut file = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```

### impl<F> [NamedUtf8TempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)<F>

Get the temporary file’s path.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-2)Security

Referring to a temporary file’s path may not be secure in all cases. Please read the security section on the top level documentation of this type for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
let file = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
println!("{}", file.path());
```
Close and remove the temporary file.

Use this if you want to detect errors in deleting the file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

If the file cannot be deleted, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
let file = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
// By closing the `NamedUtf8TempFile` explicitly, we can check that it
// has been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the file will still be deleted when `file` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the file
// succeeded.
file.close()?;
```
Persist the temporary file at the target path.

If a file exists at the target path, persist will atomically replace it. If this method
fails, it will return `self` in the resulting [ Utf8PersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8PersistError.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

- This method accepts `AsRef<Path>`rather than`AsRef<Utf8Path>`because it returns the underlying file type`F`.
- Temporary files cannot be persisted across filesystems.
- Neither the file contents nor the containing directory are synchronized, so the update may
not yet have reached the disk when `persist`returns.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-3)Security

This method persists the temporary file using its path and may not be secure in the in all cases. Please read the security section on the top level documentation of this type for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-2)Errors

If the file cannot be moved to the new location, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
let file = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
let mut persisted_file = file.persist("./saved_file.txt")?;
writeln!(persisted_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```

Persist the temporary file at the target path if and only if no file exists there.

If a file exists at the target path, fail. If this method fails, it will return `self` in
the resulting [ Utf8PersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8PersistError.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#notes-1)Notes

- This method accepts `AsRef<Path>`rather than`AsRef<Utf8Path>`because it returns the underlying file type`F`.
- Temporary files cannot be persisted across filesystems.
- This method is not atomic. It can leave the original link to the temporary file behind.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-4)Security

This method persists the temporary file using its path and may not be secure in the in all cases. Please read the security section on the top level documentation of this type for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-3)Errors

If the file cannot be moved to the new location or a file already exists there, `Err` is
returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
let file = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
let mut persisted_file = file.persist_noclobber("./saved_file.txt")?;
writeln!(persisted_file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NamedUtf8TempFile-1)

### impl [NamedUtf8TempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)<[File](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)>

Securely reopen the temporary file.

This function is useful when you need multiple independent handles to the same file. It’s
perfectly fine to drop the original `NamedUtf8TempFile` while holding on to `File`s returned
by this function; the `File`s will remain usable. However, they may not be nameable.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-5)Errors

If the file cannot be reopened, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-5)Security

Unlike `File::open(my_temp_file.path())`, `NamedUtf8TempFile::reopen()` guarantees that the
re-opened file is the *same* file, even in the presence of pathological temporary file
cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
let file = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
let another_handle = file.reopen()?;
```

# Builder in camino_tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino-tempfile/latest/target-redirect/camino_tempfile/struct.Builder.html

`pub struct Builder<'a, 'b> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Create a new temporary file or directory with custom parameters.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new `Builder`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a named temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use camino_tempfile::Builder;
let named_tempfile = Builder::new()
    .prefix("my-temporary-note")
    .suffix(".txt")
    .rand_bytes(5)
    .tempfile()?;
let name = named_tempfile.path().file_name();
if let Some(name) = name {
    assert!(name.starts_with("my-temporary-note"));
    assert!(name.ends_with(".txt"));
    assert_eq!(name.len(), "my-temporary-note.txt".len() + 5);
}
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use camino_tempfile::Builder;
let dir = Builder::new()
    .prefix("my-temporary-dir")
    .rand_bytes(5)
    .tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `Utf8TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```
Create a temporary directory with a chosen prefix under a chosen folder:

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camino_tempfile/builder.rs.html#269-272)#### pub fn [permissions](https://docs.rs#method.permissions)(&mut self, permissions: [Permissions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.Permissions.html)) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camino_tempfile/builder.rs.html#269-272)

#### pub fn [permissions](https://docs.rs#method.permissions)(&mut self, permissions: [Permissions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.Permissions.html)) -> &mut Self

The permissions to create the tempfile or [tempdir](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.tempdir) with.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

By default, the permissions of tempfiles on Unix are set for it to be readable and writable by the owner only, yielding the greatest amount of security. As this method allows to widen the permissions, security would be reduced in such cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-notes)Platform Notes

[§](https://docs.rs#unix)Unix

The actual permission bits set on the tempfile or tempdir will be
affected by the `umask` applied by the underlying syscall. The actual
permission bits are calculated via `permissions & !umask`.

Permissions default to `0o600` for tempfiles and `0o777` for tempdirs.
Note, this doesn’t include effects of the current `umask`. For example,
combined with the standard umask `0o022`, the defaults yield `0o600` for
tempfiles and `0o755` for tempdirs.

[§](https://docs.rs#windows-and-others)Windows and others

This setting is unsupported and trying to set a file or directory read-only will return an error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

Create a named temporary file that is world-readable.

```
use camino_tempfile::Builder;
use std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt;
let all_read_write = std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(0o666);
let tempfile = Builder::new().permissions(all_read_write).tempfile()?;
let actual_permissions = tempfile.path().metadata()?.permissions();
assert_ne!(
    actual_permissions.mode() & !0o170000,
    0o600,
    "we get broader permissions than the default despite umask"
);
```
Create a named temporary directory that is restricted to the owner.

```
use camino_tempfile::Builder;
use std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt;
let owner_rwx = std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(0o700);
let tempdir = Builder::new().permissions(owner_rwx).tempdir()?;
let actual_permissions = tempdir.path().metadata()?.permissions();
assert_eq!(
    actual_permissions.mode() & !0o170000,
    0o700,
    "we get the narrow permissions we asked for"
);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camino_tempfile/builder.rs.html#548-553)#### pub fn [make](https://docs.rs#method.make)<F, R>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedUtf8TempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)<R>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camino_tempfile/builder.rs.html#548-553)

#### pub fn [make](https://docs.rs#method.make)<F, R>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[NamedUtf8TempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html)<R>>

Attempts to create a temporary file (or file-like object) using the
provided closure. The closure is passed a temporary file path and
returns an [ std::io::Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html). The path provided to the closure will be
inside of

[. Use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`std::env::temp_dir()`[to provide a custom temporary directory. If the closure returns one of the following errors, then another randomized file path is tried:](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.make_in)

`Builder::make_in`This can be helpful for taking full control over the file creation, but leaving the temporary file path construction up to the library. This also enables creating a temporary UNIX domain socket, since it is not possible to bind to a socket that already exists.

Note that [ Builder::append](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.append) is ignored when using

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.make)

`Builder::make`[§](https://docs.rs#security-3)Security

This has the same [security implications](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html#security) as
[ NamedUtf8TempFile](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html), but with additional caveats. Specifically, it is up
to the closure to ensure that the file does not exist and that such a
check is

*atomic*. Otherwise, a

[time-of-check to time-of-use bug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-of-check_to_time-of-use)could be introduced.

For example, the following is **not** secure:

```
// This is NOT secure!
let tempfile = Builder::new().make(|path| {
    if path.is_file() {
        return Err(io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists.into());
    }
    // Between the check above and the usage below, an attacker could
    // have replaced `path` with another file, which would get truncated
    // by `File::create`.
    File::create(path)
})?;
```
Note that simply using [ std::fs::File::create](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html#method.create) alone is not correct
because it does not fail if the file already exists:

```
// This could overwrite an existing file!
let tempfile = Builder::new().make(|path| File::create(path))?;
```
For creating regular temporary files, use [ Builder::tempfile](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.tempfile) instead
to avoid these problems. This function is meant to enable more exotic
use-cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking-4)Resource leaking

See [the resource leaking](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedUtf8TempFile.html#resource-leaking) docs on `NamedUtf8TempFile`.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-4)Errors

If the closure returns any error besides
[ std::io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/error/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.AlreadyExists) or

[, then](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/error/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.AddrInUse)

`std::io::ErrorKind::AddrInUse``Err` is returned.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use std::os::unix::net::UnixListener;
let tempsock = Builder::new().make(|path| UnixListener::bind(path))?;
```

# Utf8TempPath in camino_tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino-tempfile/latest/target-redirect/camino_tempfile/struct.Utf8TempPath.html

`pub struct Utf8TempPath { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A path to a named temporary file without an open file handle.

This is useful when the temporary file needs to be used by a child process, for example.

When dropped, the temporary file is deleted.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Utf8TempPath)

### impl [Utf8TempPath](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempPath.html)

Close and remove the temporary file.

Use this if you want to detect errors in deleting the file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the file cannot be deleted, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
let file = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
// Close the file, but keep the path to it around.
let path = file.into_temp_path();
// By closing the `Utf8TempPath` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly, the
// file will still be deleted when `file` goes out of scope, but we
// won't know whether deleting the file succeeded.
path.close()?;
```
Persist the temporary file at the target path.

If a file exists at the target path, persist will atomically replace it. If this method
fails, it will return `self` in the resulting [ Utf8PathPersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8PathPersistError.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

- This method accepts `AsRef<Path>`rather than`AsRef<Utf8Path>`, because in the success case it does not return anything.
- Temporary files cannot be persisted across filesystems.
- Neither the file contents nor the containing directory are synchronized, so the update may
not yet have reached the disk when `persist`returns.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

Only use this method if you’re positive that a temporary file cleaner won’t have deleted your file. Otherwise, you might end up persisting an attacker controlled file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

If the file cannot be moved to the new location, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
let mut file = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
let path = file.into_temp_path();
path.persist("./saved_file.txt")?;
```

#### pub fn [persist_noclobber](https://docs.rs#method.persist_noclobber)<P: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)>>(
    self,
    new_path: P,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [Utf8PathPersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8PathPersistError.html)>

Persist the temporary file at the target path if and only if no file exists there.

If a file exists at the target path, fail. If this method fails, it will return `self` in
the resulting [ Utf8PathPersistError](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8PathPersistError.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#notes-1)Notes

- This method accepts `AsRef<Path>`rather than`AsRef<Utf8Path>`, because in the success case it does not return anything.
- Temporary files cannot be persisted across filesystems.
- This method is not atomic. It can leave the original link to the temporary file behind.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-1)Security

Only use this method if you’re positive that a temporary file cleaner won’t have deleted your file. Otherwise, you might end up persisting an attacker controlled file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-2)Errors

If the file cannot be moved to the new location or a file already exists there, `Err` is
returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::NamedUtf8TempFile;
let mut file = NamedUtf8TempFile::new()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
let path = file.into_temp_path();
path.persist_noclobber("./saved_file.txt")?;
```

#### pub fn [disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs#method.disable_cleanup)(&mut self, disable_cleanup: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Disable cleanup of the temporary file. If `disable_cleanup` is `true`,
the temporary file will not be deleted when this `Utf8TempPath` is
dropped. This method is equivalent to calling
[ Builder::disable_cleanup](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.disable_cleanup) when creating the original

`Utf8TempPath`,
which see for relevant warnings.**NOTE:** this method is primarily useful for testing/debugging. If you
want to simply turn a temporary file-path into a non-temporary
file-path, prefer [ Utf8TempPath::keep](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempPath.html#method.keep).

[Source](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/camino/lib.rs.html#641)

#### pub fn [as_std_path](https://docs.rs#method.as_std_path)(&self) -> &[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)

Converts a `Utf8Path` to a [ Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html).

This is equivalent to the `AsRef<&Path> for &Utf8Path` impl, but may aid in type inference.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
use std::path::Path;
let utf8_path = Utf8Path::new("foo.txt");
let std_path: &Path = utf8_path.as_std_path();
assert_eq!(std_path.to_str(), Some("foo.txt"));
// Convert back to a Utf8Path.
let new_utf8_path = Utf8Path::from_path(std_path).unwrap();
assert_eq!(new_utf8_path, "foo.txt");
```
Yields the underlying [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html) slice.

Unlike [ Path::to_str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html#method.to_str), this always returns a slice because the contents of a

`Utf8Path`
are guaranteed to be valid UTF-8.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
let s = Utf8Path::new("foo.txt").as_str();
assert_eq!(s, "foo.txt");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/camino/lib.rs.html#720)#### pub fn [is_absolute](https://docs.rs#method.is_absolute)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/camino/lib.rs.html#720)

#### pub fn [is_absolute](https://docs.rs#method.is_absolute)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns `true` if the `Utf8Path` is absolute, i.e., if it is independent of
the current directory.

-
On Unix, a path is absolute if it starts with the root, so `is_absolute`and`has_root`
-
On Windows, a path is absolute if it has a prefix and starts with the root: `c:\windows`is absolute, while`c:temp`and`\temp`are not.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
assert!(!Utf8Path::new("foo.txt").is_absolute());
```
Returns `true` if the `Utf8Path` has a root.

-
On Unix, a path has a root if it begins with `/`.
-
On Windows, a path has a root if it: - has no prefix and begins with a separator, e.g., `\windows`
- has a prefix followed by a separator, e.g., `c:\windows`but not`c:windows`
- has any non-disk prefix, e.g., `\\server\share`

- has no prefix and begins with a separator, e.g.,

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
assert!(Utf8Path::new("/etc/passwd").has_root());
```
Returns the `Path` without its final component, if there is one.

Returns [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if the path terminates in a root or prefix.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
let path = Utf8Path::new("/foo/bar");
let parent = path.parent().unwrap();
assert_eq!(parent, Utf8Path::new("/foo"));
let grand_parent = parent.parent().unwrap();
assert_eq!(grand_parent, Utf8Path::new("/"));
assert_eq!(grand_parent.parent(), None);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/camino/lib.rs.html#820)#### pub fn [ancestors](https://docs.rs#method.ancestors)(&self) -> [Utf8Ancestors](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Ancestors.html)<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/camino/lib.rs.html#820)

#### pub fn [ancestors](https://docs.rs#method.ancestors)(&self) -> [Utf8Ancestors](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Ancestors.html)<'_>

Produces an iterator over `Utf8Path` and its ancestors.

The iterator will yield the `Utf8Path` that is returned if the [ parent](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html#method.parent) method is used zero
or more times. That means, the iterator will yield

`&self`, `&self.parent().unwrap()`,
`&self.parent().unwrap().parent().unwrap()` and so on. If the [method returns](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html#method.parent)

`parent`[, the iterator will do likewise. The iterator will always yield at least one value, namely](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None``&self`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
let mut ancestors = Utf8Path::new("/foo/bar").ancestors();
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Utf8Path::new("/foo/bar")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Utf8Path::new("/foo")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Utf8Path::new("/")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), None);
let mut ancestors = Utf8Path::new("../foo/bar").ancestors();
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Utf8Path::new("../foo/bar")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Utf8Path::new("../foo")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Utf8Path::new("..")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), Some(Utf8Path::new("")));
assert_eq!(ancestors.next(), None);
```
Returns the final component of the `Utf8Path`, if there is one.

If the path is a normal file, this is the file name. If it’s the path of a directory, this is the directory name.

Returns [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if the path terminates in

`..`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
assert_eq!(Some("bin"), Utf8Path::new("/usr/bin/").file_name());
assert_eq!(Some("foo.txt"), Utf8Path::new("tmp/foo.txt").file_name());
assert_eq!(Some("foo.txt"), Utf8Path::new("foo.txt/.").file_name());
assert_eq!(Some("foo.txt"), Utf8Path::new("foo.txt/.//").file_name());
assert_eq!(None, Utf8Path::new("foo.txt/..").file_name());
assert_eq!(None, Utf8Path::new("/").file_name());
```

If `base` is not a prefix of `self` (i.e., [ starts_with](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html#method.starts_with)

#### pub fn [starts_with](https://docs.rs#method.starts_with)(&self, base: impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)>) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Determines whether `base` is a prefix of `self`.

Only considers whole path components to match.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
let path = Utf8Path::new("/etc/passwd");
assert!(path.starts_with("/etc"));
assert!(path.starts_with("/etc/"));
assert!(path.starts_with("/etc/passwd"));
assert!(path.starts_with("/etc/passwd/")); // extra slash is okay
assert!(path.starts_with("/etc/passwd///")); // multiple extra slashes are okay
assert!(!path.starts_with("/e"));
assert!(!path.starts_with("/etc/passwd.txt"));
assert!(!Utf8Path::new("/etc/foo.rs").starts_with("/etc/foo"));
```
Determines whether `child` is a suffix of `self`.

Only considers whole path components to match.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
let path = Utf8Path::new("/etc/resolv.conf");
assert!(path.ends_with("resolv.conf"));
assert!(path.ends_with("etc/resolv.conf"));
assert!(path.ends_with("/etc/resolv.conf"));
assert!(!path.ends_with("/resolv.conf"));
assert!(!path.ends_with("conf")); // use .extension() instead
```
Extracts the stem (non-extension) portion of [ self.file_name](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html#method.file_name).

The stem is:

- `None`
- The entire file name if there is no embedded `.`;
- The entire file name if the file name begins with `.`and has no other`.`s within;
- Otherwise, the portion of the file name before the final `.`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
assert_eq!("foo", Utf8Path::new("foo.rs").file_stem().unwrap());
assert_eq!("foo.tar", Utf8Path::new("foo.tar.gz").file_stem().unwrap());
```
Extracts the extension of [ self.file_name](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html#method.file_name), if possible.

The extension is:

- `None`
- `None`- `.`;
- `None`- `.`and has no other- `.`s within;
- Otherwise, the portion of the file name after the final `.`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
assert_eq!("rs", Utf8Path::new("foo.rs").extension().unwrap());
assert_eq!("gz", Utf8Path::new("foo.tar.gz").extension().unwrap());
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/camino/lib.rs.html#1108)#### pub fn [components](https://docs.rs#method.components)(&self) -> [Utf8Components](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Components.html)<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/camino/lib.rs.html#1108)

#### pub fn [components](https://docs.rs#method.components)(&self) -> [Utf8Components](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Components.html)<'_>

Produces an iterator over the [ Utf8Component](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/enum.Utf8Component.html)s of the path.

When parsing the path, there is a small amount of normalization:

-
Repeated separators are ignored, so `a/b`and`a//b`both have`a`and`b`as components.
-
Occurrences of `.`are normalized away, except if they are at the beginning of the path. For example,`a/./b`,`a/b/`,`a/b/.`and`a/b`all have`a`and`b`as components, but`./a/b`starts with an additional`CurDir`
-
A trailing slash is normalized away, `/a/b`and`/a/b/`are equivalent.

Note that no other normalization takes place; in particular, `a/c`
and `a/b/../c` are distinct, to account for the possibility that `b`
is a symbolic link (so its parent isn’t `a`).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-23)Examples

```
use camino::{Utf8Component, Utf8Path};
let mut components = Utf8Path::new("/tmp/foo.txt").components();
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Utf8Component::RootDir));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Utf8Component::Normal("tmp")));
assert_eq!(components.next(), Some(Utf8Component::Normal("foo.txt")));
assert_eq!(components.next(), None)
```
Produces an iterator over the path’s components viewed as [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)
slices.

For more information about the particulars of how the path is separated
into components, see [ components](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html#method.components).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-24)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
let mut it = Utf8Path::new("/tmp/foo.txt").iter();
assert_eq!(it.next(), Some(std::path::MAIN_SEPARATOR.to_string().as_str()));
assert_eq!(it.next(), Some("tmp"));
assert_eq!(it.next(), Some("foo.txt"));
assert_eq!(it.next(), None)
```

Returns `true` if the path points at an existing entity.

Warning: this method may be error-prone, consider using [ try_exists()](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html#method.try_exists) instead!
It also has a risk of introducing time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) bugs.

This function will traverse symbolic links to query information about the
destination file. In case of broken symbolic links this will return `false`.

If you cannot access the directory containing the file, e.g., because of a
permission error, this will return `false`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-33)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
assert!(!Utf8Path::new("does_not_exist.txt").exists());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#see-also)See Also

This is a convenience function that coerces errors to false. If you want to
check errors, call [ fs::metadata](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/fn.metadata.html).

[Source](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/camino/lib.rs.html#1385)#### pub fn [try_exists](https://docs.rs#method.try_exists)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)>

#### pub fn [try_exists](https://docs.rs#method.try_exists)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)>

Returns `Ok(true)` if the path points at an existing entity.

This function will traverse symbolic links to query information about the
destination file. In case of broken symbolic links this will return `Ok(false)`.

As opposed to the [ exists()](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html#method.exists) method, this one doesn’t silently ignore errors
unrelated to the path not existing. (E.g. it will return

`Err(_)` in case of permission
denied on some of the parent directories.)Note that while this avoids some pitfalls of the `exists()` method, it still can not
prevent time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) bugs. You should only use it in scenarios
where those bugs are not an issue.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-34)Examples

```
use camino::Utf8Path;
assert!(!Utf8Path::new("does_not_exist.txt").try_exists().expect("Can't check existence of file does_not_exist.txt"));
assert!(Utf8Path::new("/root/secret_file.txt").try_exists().is_err());
```

# tempdir_in in camino_tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino-tempfile/latest/target-redirect/camino_tempfile/fn.tempdir_in.html

`pub fn tempdir_in<P: `[AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Utf8Path](https://docs.rs/camino/1.1.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camino/struct.Utf8Path.html)>>(dir: P) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/type.Result.html)<[Utf8TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html)>## Expand description

Create a new temporary directory in a specific directory.

The `tempdir_in` function creates a directory in the specified directory and returns a
[ Utf8TempDir](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html). The directory will be automatically deleted when the

[’s destructor is run.](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8TempDir.html)

`Utf8TempDir`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

See [the resource leaking](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html#resource-leaking) docs on `Utf8TempDir`.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the directory can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::tempdir_in;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{self, Write};
// Create a directory inside of the current directory.
let dir = tempdir_in(".")?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// `tmp_dir` goes out of scope, the directory as well as
// `tmp_file` will be deleted here.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

# tempfile_in in camino_tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/camino-tempfile/latest/target-redirect/camino_tempfile/fn.tempfile_in.html

## Expand description

Create a new temporary file in the specified directory.

This method accepts `AsRef<Path>` rather than `AsRef<Utf8Path>` because it returns a
[ std::fs::File](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This variant is secure/reliable in the presence of a pathological temporary file cleaner. If the
temporary file isn’t created in [ std::env::temp_dir()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/env/fn.temp_dir.html) then temporary file cleaners aren’t an
issue.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

The temporary file will be automatically removed by the OS when the last handle to it is closed. This doesn’t rely on Rust destructors being run, so will (almost) never fail to clean up the temporary file.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the file can not be created, `Err` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use camino_tempfile::tempfile_in;
use std::io::{self, Write};
// Create a file inside of the current working directory
let mut file = tempfile_in("./")?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
